title: Machine Learning Foundations
premise: The classical grounding that makes deep learning legible rather than magical, and the source of almost all evaluation intuition. Everything you learned to measure in AIE-102 was invented here, on models small enough to see through. A model you have implemented from the update rule is a model whose failures you can diagnose; one you have only called is one you can only restart.
why_here: Ninth overall and second in Block II, after the mathematics that makes the derivations readable and before the deep learning that assumes all of it. It also settles a debt: AIE-107 made you compare an LLM against a classical baseline, and a baseline you reached for out of the box is not evidence of anything until you know what it was doing.
laboratory: The same problems, taken seriously this time. Career Side Quests' requirement-versus-boilerplate line classification is a genuine supervised problem with labels you can produce in an afternoon. Indie Degree's own resource corpus is an unsupervised problem where you already computed an SVD in AIE-201 and can now ask whether the clusters agree with the components. Carpark SG's rate data is a regression problem with real messiness and a ground truth that exists.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing. The portfolio contains no classical model, no learning curve and no calibration plot; AIE-107's comparison used sklearn defaults, which evidences the ability to call a library rather than to choose one.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Judges are instructed that a from-scratch implementation which is slower and less accurate than the library is not thereby worse: the criterion is whether it matches the library's behaviour and whether the author can say where it diverges and why.

modules.title: Supervised learning, from the update rule

items.title: Regression and classification, derived
items.locator: The linear regression, normal equations and logistic regression lectures — through the derivation of the logistic update, not just its statement.

items.title: Training models
items.locator: Chapter 4, Training Models — linear regression by normal equation and by gradient descent, then logistic and softmax regression.

items.title: Linear and logistic regression from scratch
checkpoints: Linear regression by normal equation and by gradient descent, agreeing
Logistic regression implemented with its own gradient
sklearn comparison run on identical data
Divergences investigated rather than tolerated
items.brief: Implement linear regression twice — once by the normal equation, once by gradient descent — and confirm they agree. Then implement logistic regression, deriving and coding its gradient rather than importing one. Fit all three against scikit-learn on the same data and compare coefficients, not just predictions. Where the coefficients differ, find out whether it is regularisation, the intercept handling, or convergence, and say which.

items.title: Trees and ensembles
items.locator: Chapters 6 and 7 — decision trees, then bagging, random forests, and gradient boosting.

items.title: A decision tree, then a forest
checkpoints: Split criterion implemented and its value verified by hand on one node
Tree grown with a stated stopping rule
Bagging added over the tree
Variance reduction measured across seeds
items.brief: Implement a decision tree: the split criterion, the greedy search, and a stopping rule you choose deliberately. Verify the impurity calculation by hand at one node. Then wrap it in bagging and measure what averaging over bootstrap samples does to variance across random seeds. Report the variance before and after, because 'ensembles reduce variance' is a sentence everyone repeats and few have measured.

items.title: Retention: model families and what each assumes

modules.title: Bias, variance, and what the curves say

items.title: Learning theory and the bias-variance decomposition
items.locator: The bias-variance and learning theory lectures, including the discussion of where the decomposition stops being a useful picture.

items.title: Generalisation, and splitting data honestly
items.locator: The generalisation, training-and-test-sets, and validation units — particularly why a test set consulted repeatedly stops being one.

items.title: Learning curves that actually diagnose
checkpoints: An underfitting model produced and its curve recorded
An overfitting model produced and its curve recorded
Both curves plotted with training and validation on the same axes
The distinguishing feature named
items.brief: Deliberately produce one model that underfits and one that overfits the same dataset. Plot training and validation error against training set size for both. Then write the part that makes this useful later: given only the shapes of these curves, what tells them apart, and what would you do next in each case. A curve you cannot act on is decoration.

items.title: Diagnose something you actually run
checkpoints: A real model or pipeline of your own chosen and described
Curves produced from its real data
A diagnosis stated before any fix is attempted
The fix applied and re-measured, or the diagnosis retracted
items.brief: Take a model or scoring component from something you have shipped. Produce learning curves from its real data. State a diagnosis — more data, more capacity, better features, or the problem is not learnable as framed — and commit to it in writing before trying anything. Then act on it and measure. Retracting a diagnosis that the measurement refuses to support is a full-marks outcome; quietly changing it is not.

modules.title: Features, and the ways they lie

items.title: An end-to-end project, for the pipeline
items.locator: Chapter 2, End-to-End Machine Learning Project — the data preparation, transformation pipeline and custom transformer sections.

items.title: Features that earn their place
checkpoints: A baseline with raw features measured first
Each engineered feature added one at a time
Lift measured per feature against the baseline
Features with no lift removed and reported
items.brief: Take one of your own datasets. Measure a baseline on raw features before engineering anything. Then add engineered features one at a time and measure the lift of each. Report the ones that gained nothing and remove them. The deliverable is not a better model; it is a table of which ideas worked and by how much, including the ones that felt obviously right and did nothing.

items.title: Find the leak
checkpoints: A leaking feature introduced deliberately and its effect measured
The leak detected by a stated procedure rather than by knowing where it was
The procedure applied to a real pipeline of your own
items.brief: Introduce target leakage into a pipeline on purpose — a feature computed after the fact, or a scaler fitted before the split — and measure how good it makes your model look. Then design a procedure that would have caught it without knowing where it was, and run that procedure against a pipeline you actually use. Report what it found, including nothing.

items.title: Framing the problem before the features
items.locator: The chapters on framing the problem and on building a first end-to-end pipeline — where the choice of label is shown to matter more than the choice of model.

items.title: Dimensionality reduction and clustering
items.locator: Chapters 8 and 9 — PCA and its variants, then k-means, DBSCAN and Gaussian mixtures.

items.title: Cluster the corpus you already decomposed
checkpoints: The same corpus and matrix used as in AIE-201 M1.5
k chosen by a stated method before inspecting the clusters
Clusters compared against the SVD components from the earlier assignment
Agreement or disagreement reported with examples
items.brief: Reuse the term-document matrix you built for AIE-201's decomposition assignment. Cluster it, choosing k by a method you state in advance rather than by looking. Then do the thing that makes this worth doing: compare the clusters against the singular vectors you already interpreted. If they agree, say what that tells you. If they disagree, say which one you believe and why — that is the interesting outcome and it is the one people quietly drop.

items.title: Where clustering told you nothing
checkpoints: Clustering run on data with no real cluster structure
The algorithm's output shown to be confident anyway
A validity measure applied and reported
A rule written for when not to trust a clustering
items.brief: Run k-means on data you know has no cluster structure — uniform noise will do — and show that it returns clusters anyway, with a plausible-looking plot. Apply a validity measure such as silhouette and report what it says. Then write the rule you will actually use: what would have to be true before you present a clustering to anyone as a finding.

items.title: k-means, EM and PCA, derived
items.locator: The k-means, mixture-of-Gaussians with EM, and PCA lectures.

items.title: Retention: unsupervised methods and their failure to abstain
A metric chosen for a reason
checkpoints: An imbalanced problem taken or constructed, with the base rate stated
A majority-class baseline scored under every candidate metric
The chosen metric justified against the cost of each error type
The model compared against the baseline under that metric
items.brief: Take an imbalanced problem and state its base rate. Score a majority-class baseline under accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and average precision, and show which of those the baseline can win. Then choose the metric you would report, justifying it by what a false positive and a false negative actually cost in that setting — not by which is conventional.

items.title: Calibrate, and show the reliability diagram
checkpoints: Reliability diagram produced before calibration
A calibration method applied on held-out data
Diagram reproduced after, with a calibration error reported
The effect on the ranking metric checked
items.brief: Produce a reliability diagram for a classifier of yours and report its calibration error. Apply Platt scaling or isotonic regression on data the model has not seen, and reproduce the diagram. Then check what calibration did to your ranking metric — it is usually close to nothing, and knowing that calibration and discrimination are separate properties is the point of the assignment.

items.title: The baseline that should have been there
checkpoints: The AIE-107 comparison revisited with a properly built classical model
Tuning, features and metric choice documented
The verdict restated, whether or not it changes
Published and connected backwards to the earlier chapter
items.brief: Go back to the requirement-versus-boilerplate comparison from AIE-107, where the classical model was whatever scikit-learn offered by default. Rebuild it properly: chosen features, tuned hyperparameters, a metric justified for the imbalance, and calibration if it matters. Publish the result as a chapter of the public log, connected back to the original. State plainly whether the verdict changes. If a well-built classical model now beats the LLM you shipped, that is the most valuable sentence in the programme so far and it must be written down.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own submissions at defense time, answered aloud without notes.
sample_question_shapes: Your bagged trees reduced variance. By how much, and how would you know if the reduction were noise?
You reported average precision rather than ROC-AUC. Someone senior says AUC is standard. Answer them.
Your clusters disagreed with the SVD components. Which did you believe, and what would change your mind?

rubrics.integrity: If the rebuilt classical model beats the shipped LLM, that finding must be published rather than buried. Judges are instructed that a submission reaching it scores higher, not lower, and that omitting an unfavourable result is the failure this rubric exists to catch.

preconditions.check: questions generated at defense time from the author's own submissions
answered aloud without notes
recording or transcript retained

criteria.criterion: Claims are defended with the measurement behind them

levels.3: Explains how it was measured and what would have made it wrong.

criteria.criterion: Statistical care survives being pushed

levels.2: Holds the claim within its interval.
levels.3: Holds the claim within its interval and says what sample would settle it.

criteria.criterion: Disagreement is handled on the merits

levels.3: Argues from the setting and concedes where the questioner is right.

rubrics.integrity: Conceding a real error is scored as strength. A defense in which the author never yields is evidence of stubbornness rather than understanding.

completion.required: All nine assignments, the project and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on all four machine-learning skills, and is the course that makes AIE-102's evaluation vocabulary mean something mechanical rather than borrowed. FSRS then decays them.
